newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president confronts parliament over powers.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president confronts parliament over powers.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko on Tuesday rejected a vote by parliament to prevent him boosting his powers in the former Soviet republic of Belarus.
Lukashenko issued a decree saying he would only need the people's support in a November 24 referendum to extend his term.
His decree clearly contradicted a constitutional court ruling on Monday which said only parliament had the right to decide if the referendum should be obeyed.
Parliament had voted to declare the referendum "consultative" -- meaning it would have no mandatory, constitutional force.
The president's proposed draft constitution would, if approved, allow him to recommence his five-year term from the day of the referendum, extending it by more than two years.
"If more than 50 percent of citizens back this constitution, it will become mandatory and the results will have legal force," state television quoted a Lukashenko decree as saying late on Tuesday.
"The results will in that case be final and will need no legal confirmation," it added.
Lukashenko has ignored a string of constitutional court rulings and parliamentary votes since taking the helm of one of the smallest former Soviet republics.

He will also ask the nation for authority to create an upper house of parliament partly appointed by him, and to name all court judges, half the constitutional court and half the commission which monitors and holds elections.
The 44-year-old former collective farm chief had threatened to dissolve parliament if the court declared the referendum unconstitutional.
The court stepped back from this but the row was clearly far from diffused on Monday and it moved into a new phase with Tuesday's parliamentary vote and Lukashenko's decree.
Lukashenko has been battling a majority of deputies over the referendum and many other issues since he won a landslide victory on a platform of fighting crime in July 1994.
Since then he has suspended trade unions, closed newspapers and frozen the country's privatisation programme.
He has drawn criticism from the West for his increasingly authoritarian rule and lending bodies have suspended credits pending faster reforms.
